newsitem.title: MONACO: ATHLETICS-LEWIS ACCUSES U.S. OF HUSHING UP DOPING.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-LEWIS ACCUSES U.S. OF HUSHING UP DOPING.

text.p: Carl Lewis accused athletics authorities of trying to hush up the abuse of performance-enhancing drugs in U.S. sport after it emerged on Wednesday that two more American athletes had been caught doping.
A few days after a doping scandal involving leading American athletes Sandra Farmer-Patrick and Mary Slaney, athletics sources said two other American athletes had tested positive for banned drugs.
Speaking by telephone from Houston, the United States' most successful athlete launched a fierce attack on his country's track and field chiefs when he heard the news.
"There is no question in my mind that they have more knowledge about the drug problem than they are telling the public," Lewis said.

"The problem (in U.S. athletics) now is that the structure has broken down and the doping problem is being ignored and sometimes supported...They are overlooking the drug problem and, in some cases, they may have even tried to protect athletes."
International Amateur Athletic Federation (IAAF) officials attending a meeting here were unable to confirm the two new positive tests.
Sources close to the cases were unable to name the substances involved or when the tests were held. But they said U.S. officials were expected to inform the IAAF of the tests in the next few days.
"There are two new positive tests in addition to the Farmer-Patrick and Mary Slaney cases," one source told Reuters. "They are not big-name athletes but definitely from the United States."
The emergence of the positive tests is a further blow to American athletics at a time when authorities are under fire for their handling of drug-testing procedures.

U.S. Track and Field authorities were criticised by the IAAF on Tuesday for dragging their feet over the cases of Farmer-Patrick and Slaney who tested positive several months before last year's Atlanta Olympics.
Farmer-Patrick was allowed to take part in the Atlanta Games and has only just been banned for four years for steroid abuse.
The Slaney case has yet to be concluded almost a year after she was found to have high levels of the banned substance testosterone in the body during a test at the U.S. trials.

Lewis, who was linked up by telephone to a news conference in Monaco to support Stockholm's bid for the 2004 Games, said there was now a great deal of scepticism among the public because of the problem of performance-enhancing drugs.
"There is a great level of cynicism amongst the public which has made it 10 times worse," Lewis said. "Sport is not about performance. It is about competition."
Former U.S. triple jumper Willie Banks, who was at the news conference, said he could barely believe what was happening with the drug scandals.
"It is a terrible blow for the sport," he said. "It is hard to believe it with Slaney. I don't believe she would try to cheat. She is too good a person for that."
